## 2026-09-17 — the name-collision audit, closed

Last tick left "~38 remaining two- and three-way collisions are unexamined" as
an honest caveat. This closes it: **outside the template and CRT families there
are 17 names over 42 functions, and every one is now classified.** No further
renames are warranted.

Each was classified from structure rather than by eye — address adjacency, size,
and a fingerprint of the set of functions each body calls:

| group | names | why it is not a defect |
|---|---|---|
| `AQ_StorageUpdater__Init` x10 | 1 | **was** a defect; fixed in v0.1.269. Still visible in the dump only because `rebuilt_dumps=0` — the Ghidra project has the new names |
| adjacent, identical size, identical fingerprint | 4 | **MSVC adjustor thunks** for multiple inheritance — `IGObj::RaiseEvent`, and `CGObjCOS_Summoned::{ExpandInventory, IsAccomplishedCollectionBook_Theme, IsRegisteredCollectionBook_Item}`. Two entry points, one adjusting `this` |
| 5-byte member of a pair | 1 | a `jmp` thunk — `Assert_BreakIfDebugger` at `005ecf60` (5 bytes) in front of `00964b60` (123) |
| CRT | 3 | `_atol`, `_clearerr_s`, and `FID_conflict:__atoflt_l`, which is Ghidra's own marker rather than a name this project chose |
| different arity or argument types | 6 | overloads — `CGObjCOS_Summoned::RaiseEvent`, `CGObjPC::ExpandInventory`, the three `CGStorage__*` pairs, the two `CGObjPC::*CollectionBook*` accessors |
| `CGameWorld__SendMsgToGameWorldAllianceUser` x2 | 1 | **the engine's own ambiguity** — see below |

### The one worth reading: the binary reuses a name

`005ec900` and `005eca40` are both 299 bytes and byte-for-byte parallel except a
single call — `FUN_004ea630` against `FUN_004ea580` — and **both carry the same
log string**:

	"CGameWorld::SendMsgToGameWorldAllianceUser() - Cant get client context from PC!!!"

So the duplicate name came from the engine, not from this project: the developer
copy-pasted the message into two near-identical broadcasters. The two 16-byte
accessors that distinguish them both read the same pointer at PC `+0x1cbc` and
tail-call different getters (`005e4390` against `005d0e90`), so the pair differs
only in which id it filters recipients by.

**No rename**: inventing two distinct names would replace the binary's own word
with a guess about which is guild and which is alliance, and the accessors'
return values were not read. Recorded instead so the next collision audit does
not flag it again.

*Small bonus:* PC `+0x1cbc` is a social-context pointer, and it is the same
field `GObjPC::IsKilledByPlayer` gates on — which is why that function also
calls `005e4390`.

**Net: zero naming defects remain among the collisions.** The 323
`CChunkAllocatorST__AllocItemBlock` functions and the CRT duplicates stay as
they are, because a template instantiated per type genuinely does share one
name.

## 2026-09-17 — the dumps could never notice a rename

`STATUS` has reported **`rebuilt_dumps=0` on every tick of this session**, during
which about a hundred names were applied to the Ghidra projects. That is not a
coincidence and it is not the cron misbehaving: `re_tick.sh` could not detect
the change, by construction.

The staleness test was

	if [ ! -f "$out/DONE" ] || [ "$bin" -nt "$out/DONE" ]; then

— *is the binary newer than the dump?* The binary is a fixed artifact from
2026-09-14 and never changes, so that question could only ever answer no. What
changes when a name is applied is the **Ghidra project**, and nothing looked at
it.

Measured before fixing, which is what turned a suspicion into a defect:

| | |
|---|---|
| `SR_GameServer.exe` mtime | 2026-09-14 00:48 (fixed) |
| `/var/tmp/decomp_server/DONE` | 2026-09-16 19:39 |
| newest file in `/home/ghidra/re_server` | **2026-09-17 00:21** — the last name-application run |

The project was five hours ahead of the dump and the check could not see it.

**This is "the metric that could not move" from the other end.** That entry
recorded names going into docs while nothing wrote them back into the project.
This is names going into the project while nothing pulls them into the dump —
and the dump is what every grep, every probe and every coverage count in this
ledger actually reads. It cost this session directly: the collision audit read
ten functions still called `AQ_StorageUpdater__Init` **after** they had been
renamed, and the discrepancy had to be explained rather than avoided.

**Fixed.** `redump` now also rebuilds when the project's newest file is newer
than a `PROJSTAMP` written into the dump directory. Two details matter:

- the stamp is captured **after** the rebuild, not before — `analyzeHeadless`
  touches the project even with `-readOnly`, and stamping it beforehand would
  make every tick see a change and rebuild forever;
- `rm -rf "$out"` wipes the dump directory, so the stamp has to live there and
  be rewritten each time, which is exactly what makes a missing stamp mean
  "rebuild".

Verified by dry-running the new condition before trusting it (`project=…00:21:45
stamp=0 -> rebuild=YES` for both dumps), then running the tick to bring the
dumps level with the names.

The script is version-controlled at `client/tools/re_tick.sh`; the repo copy was
**byte-identical** to the box's before this change, so there was no prior drift
to reconcile, and it now carries the fix.

### Verified after the fix

The catch-up run finished and the fix is confirmed end to end:

	last_tick=2026-09-17T00:51:06   finished=2026-09-17T01:00:02
	rebuilt_dumps=1
	server_dump=functions=34113 failed=0 seconds=200 shards=18
	client_dump=functions=43460 failed=0 seconds=326 shards=22

**`rebuilt_dumps=1` is the first non-zero of the session.** Checked in the
rebuilt dump rather than assumed:

- all fifteen sampled names applied this session are present —
  the ten storage operations, `StrLevelDamageRatio`, `IntLevelDamageRatio`,
  `SelectDaraParamForDamageType`, `ResolveDeathCause`, `IsKilledByPlayer`;
- **zero** functions still carry `AQ_StorageUpdater__Init`, so the ten-way
  collision is gone from the dump as well as the project;
- server functions with a real leaf name: **1,718 -> 1,778**.

That last number is the one worth keeping in view. It is the *leaf-name* count —
a function is counted only when its own name is real, not when it merely sits in
a named class — which is why it reads 5.2% where the class-qualified figure
reads 62%. Both are true and they measure different things; quoting the second
as "named" is the trap.

## 2026-09-17 — a typo in the engine's source hid four stubs, and a circular validation

Hunting the "second seed source" the last entry called for. It found one, small
and exact — and, more usefully, caught a flaw in how I had been validating.

### The `## Illegal ##` harvest missed a typo variant

The base-class stub strings are not uniform. Counted:

| leading hashes | strings | still unnamed |
|---|---|---|
| `##` | **208** | 0 |
| `#` | **6** | **4** |

The original harvest grepped `"## Illegal ##"`, so the six one-hash strings were
invisible to it. They also spell the class `IGOBJ` rather than `IGObj`. Four
were still unnamed and are now applied — `IGObj::EngageBuffSkill`,
`NotifyClientAPIconStatus`, `IsActiveBuff`, `GetRemainSkillPoint` — each
confirmed by its **body** and not merely its label: 34-39 bytes of
`log("# Illegal ## IGOBJ::<Method> TypeID: %u"); Assert(); return;`, where the
string is the function's whole purpose rather than something it mentions.

Two entries this session now turn on the same thing: an empty or short result is
a fact about the pattern. `"## Illegal ##"` and `GetParam` were both *good*
probes that quietly under-covered.

### Where the ten-way collision came from

Visible now that the dump carries last tick's corrections: each of those ten
functions contains the literal string `"AQ_StorageUpdater::Init"`. One shared
log label, taken by an earlier pass as ten names. The same shape as
`SendMsgToGameWorldAllianceUser`, where two functions share one message.

**So the rule is: a `Class::Method` label names a function only when exactly one
function carries it.** Measured: of **409** distinct labels found inside
function bodies, **23 are carried by more than one function** and are unsafe as
names; 386 are unique.

### The validation was circular, and 100% was not evidence

Testing that rule against already-named functions gave **360 agree, 0 differ**.
That number is worthless, and noticing why is the point: the functions it tested
are largely ones an earlier pass named *from these very labels*, so the sample
was selected by the rule under test.

The independent check exposed it immediately. `FUN_00469100` carries a unique
label `GObjPC::DumpItemWithOptions` — and is a **7,622-byte logging function**
full of item-serial, drop, gold and token messages. It is not that method; it
merely mentions it. A rule scored at "100%" would have renamed it.

**What survives**: the four stubs above, because their evidence is structural
(body shape) rather than the label alone. The remaining unique-label candidates
are not applied, because the only thing recommending them is a validation that
cannot see its own blind spot.

**For the next lever**: when a naming rule is scored against already-named
functions, check first whether those names came from the rule. If they did, the
score measures nothing.

## 2026-09-17 — the self-naming-stub lever is provably done, and the queue was lying

### The stub lever, closed by completeness rather than by giving up

Generalised last tick's find from a string pattern to a **body shape**: any
function of 90 bytes or less whose *only* string literal carries a
`Class::Method`. That catches a self-naming stub however the message is worded,
which is the fragility that had already bitten twice (`## Illegal ##` missing the
one-hash variant, `GetParam` missing `EvaluateParam`).

	tiny functions whose only string carries a Class::Method:  215
	  already named:                                           215
	  still unnamed:                                             0

**Zero remain.** The wording breakdown confirms why the generalisation was
needed: 206 say `## Illegal ##`, **4 say `# Illegal ##`**, 4 have no prefix at
all, and one says `DISCONNECT FROM`. A pattern-based harvest would have to guess
all four spellings; a shape-based one does not.

### Three of seven queue items misstated their own status

The queue's header says *"Ordered by value. Each line names the next concrete
probe, so a cold start can pick one up without re-deriving anything."* That is
exactly what makes a stale line expensive, and **this session lost part of two
ticks to one**. Audited against the shipped code:

| item | said | actually |
|---|---|---|
| 2 Death penalty | "recovered, deliberately NOT shipped" | shipped since **v0.1.164**; the last blocker closed in v0.1.258. The header contradicted its own body |
| 3 Combat damage model | "the model is not yet shipped… srrevamp still runs `base + bonus - defence`" | `combat.MitigateDamage` has carried the real shape for many tags; `ResolveBlow` runs the engine's stages 4, 13, 14, 16 in order |
| 4 Berserk numbers | "(fill 8/hit, 20 s, +50 %) — ours" | **wrong on two of three.** Duration is 60 s and recovered; the multiplier is x2 and recovered twice over; `Orbs = 5` is recovered. Only the fill rate and the 0..100 scale are ours |

All three headers are corrected in place, and item 4's "next probe" — chase

**The pattern worth keeping:** a ledger entry describes the moment it was
written, and the queue is the one place where that is actively harmful. When an
item closes, the *header* has to move, not just a note in the body — a cold
start reads the list, not the paragraphs.

## 2026-09-17 — the audit told readers to distrust the evidence base

With the work queue emptied, the other half of the goal is
`docs/GROUNDING_AUDIT.md` — the document that answers "is anything dressed up as
recovered?". Its own closing section, *"What is genuinely still assumed (summary
for the next pass)"*, had two entries and **both were stale**. One of them
mattered a great deal.

### "SR_GameServer.exe is a third-party emulator bundle, not authoritative"

That sentence sat in the audit since 2026-09-11 and told every later reader to
discount the single artifact most of this project's recovered values come from —
the damage pipeline, the death-cause enum, passive regeneration, the
`_RefObjCommon` column map, the param registry, all of it. Measured rather than
argued:

| evidence | result |
|---|---|
| strings naming `D:\WORK2005\Source\SilkroadOnline\Server\` | **55** |
| distinct Joymax **source filenames** among them | **52** |
| PE TimeDateStamp | 2011-08-08 |
| linker version | **8.0** (Visual Studio 2005, matching a `WORK2005` tree) |
| RTTI classes in Joymax's naming | 1,882 |
| `## Illegal ##` stubs naming `IGObj` methods | 208 |

Those filenames reach the binary through `__FILE__` in the assert macro **at
compile time**. A third party writing an emulator from scratch cannot end up
with 52 of Joymax's own source filenames, nor with their internal class names.
**The binary is Joymax's own build.**

**The true half is kept and separated**: a redistributed server *bundle* is
third-party, and the DATA shipped with it — rates, tables, DB contents — may be
modded, which this project already records for the VSRO package. A Joymax binary
does not make the bundled data authoritative. And the limit is stated: no
integrity check was run, so this is a claim about provenance, not about
byte-for-byte purity.

*"Level-up refills HP; derived stats (maxHP/maxMP from level+Str/Int) — the
biggest remaining ground."* It is in the grounded table at the top of this file:

### The pattern, now seen three times in two ticks

The work queue misstated three of seven items; the grounding audit misstated
both of its remaining ones. Both documents are *summaries pointing forward*, and
both decayed while the detailed entries below them stayed correct. The detail is
append-only and self-correcting; the summary is not, and nothing was re-reading

**So: when a value moves from open to recovered, the summary that lists it as

## 2026-09-17 — a tracker that cannot rot

The naming metric was measuring the wrong thing and saying so out loud was
overdue: the server has 34,113 functions, **~1,977 distinct addresses have ever
been cited across all of this project's docs**, and those produced the entire
grounded value set. The other ~32,000 are the CRT, template instantiations, and
code no reimplementation touches one function at a time. "4% named" made a
nearly-finished job look barely started.

**`docs/SYSTEMS.md` replaces it.** The unit is a system, and a system is
*specified* when it clears the bar `damage_pipeline.md` clears: entry points
named, an ordered spec with citations, every value grounded or disclosed with a
proven reason.

**The denominator is derived from the binary rather than invented.**
`SR_GameServer.exe` carries **1,209 distinct RTTI type descriptors**, of which
**1,177 are game classes**. Clustering them by family gives the surface area of
each system — and shows why a class count is not a system count: **346 of those
classes are `QNO_*` quest scripts**, instances of one handler pattern with seven
`COn*` event types. Specifying the pattern covers all 346.

Opening count: **11 specified, 7 partial, 15 open, of 33.**

### Why it is a test and not a document

Both of this project's forward-looking summaries rotted, and both were corrected
the same day: the work queue listed three of seven items as open after they had
shipped, and the grounding audit told readers the server binary was not
authoritative. The detailed entries never rotted — they are append-only, and a
new one corrects an old one in place. **Summaries decay because they make claims
about the present, and nothing re-reads them.**

So `internal/systems` parses the table on every `go test` run and fails when:

- a row cites a spec document that does not exist,
- a row claims SPECIFIED without one,
- a row claims OPEN while a spec exists — the rot that actually happened,
- an anchor identifier has vanished from `server/`,
- the prose headline disagrees with its own table.

**That last check earned its place inside one edit.** The first draft of
SYSTEMS.md said "11 of 34 specified, 7 partial, 16 open" above a table holding
33 rows with 15 open — a summary drifting from its own table, in the file whose
entire purpose is to stop summaries drifting. The test caught it before the
commit.

## 2026-09-17 — first system off the new tracker: quest scripting

`docs/SYSTEMS.md` went live this tick and quest scripting was the first OPEN row
taken. It went SPECIFIED and then **straight back to PARTIAL in the same
session**, which is the tracker doing its job. **11 specified, 8 partial, 14
open, of 33.**

**The denominator was wrong and the user caught it.** The first pass wrote "153
quests". 153 is the count of *compiled* quests; `questdata.txt` holds **696**.
So roughly a fifth of quests are scripted in C++ and four fifths are not, and
the spec had quietly generalised from the scripted fifth to the whole system.

**The previous note described a third of the system.** It recorded a
"SetupQuest / OnUpdate / OnDead triple". Counting the nested handler classes
gives the real lifecycle — **15 generic events**:

	OnSetupQuest OnEnterWorld OnUpdate OnLeaveWorld OnInstanceInvitaionAnswered
	OnEventZoneEntered OnAfterActivated OnPartyStatusChanged OnAbortQuest
	OnPreUseItem OnDead OnTimer OnTimer_Second OnScriptStarted OnBodyModeChanged

plus **12 named per-target kill hooks** — `OnDeadForGeneral1..4`,
`OnDeadForSoldier_1_1/2_1/2_2`, `OnDeadForGhost`, `OnDeadForBlackSnake`,
`OnDeadForWhiteSnake`, `OnDeadForFlameMaster`, `OnDeadForEventMonster`.

Those hooks are the strongest evidence yet for "objectives are code": a quest
that needs *kill these four named generals* does not fill in a table row, it
compiles four classes.

**The structure**: `CQNO_<NAME> : CBasicQuest : CQuestBase : IQuest` for the
quest, `COn<Event> : CEVENTHandler` for each handler, the handler's body at
vtable slot 1. The 346 `QNO_*` classes resolve as **153 quests + 193 nested
handlers**, and only **29 quests carry handlers at all** — the other 124 are
ordinary fetch-and-report quests the generic machinery serves.

**Why this counts as specified without reading 29 quest bodies:** the lifecycle
is what generalises and what an implementation has to expose. A quest engine
matching this one offers these 15 hooks plus a per-target kill hook and lets a
quest bind the ones it needs — a concrete interface derived from the engine
rather than a guess. What any individual quest *does* is 29 classes' worth of
reading that nothing needs until srrevamp ships those quests, and the spec says
so rather than implying coverage it does not have.

`OnBodyModeChanged` is worth noting on its own: it is the same body-mode enum
berserk rides on (`IGObj::SetBodyMode`, slot 198), so a quest can react to a
player going berserk. Two systems recovered a week apart turning out to share a
mechanism is the kind of thing the tracker should surface more of.

### The 543, and a conclusion that needed qualifying

Checking the denominator turned up the real open question. Of 696 quests, 153
have a compiled class (145 matching a `questdata` codename directly). The other
**543 have no compiled class — and no objective row either**:

| file | rows | what it actually holds |
|---|---|---|
| `questdata.txt` | 696 | id, codename, required level, title, `SN_*` text ids. A scan of all 12 columns for `MOB_`/`ITEM_`/`NPC_` codenames returns **nothing** |
| `questcontentsdata.txt` | 989 | the quest's **description text** — up to eight `SN_CON_*` string-id slots at cols 5-12, plus chain links. Again no mob, item or count |

`questcontentsdata.txt` is worth naming explicitly because it looks like the
objectives table this project has repeatedly concluded does not exist, and it is
not one: it is the words shown in the quest window.

So "objectives are code" holds for the scripted fifth and is **unestablished for
the other 543**. *Next probe:* read `DB_Load_RefQuest` (`0x008341b0`) and see
which columns it binds — this project has only ever inferred `_REFQUEST`'s
contents from its file counterpart. If it carries objective columns, the
standing conclusion needs qualifying rather than overturning.

**Why this is a good outcome rather than a retraction.** The lifecycle recovered
this tick — 15 events, 12 per-target kill hooks, `CEVENTHandler` slot-1 dispatch
— is unaffected and is the durable half. What changed is that the row now says
which four fifths of the system it does not cover, instead of implying it covers
all of it. PARTIAL exists for exactly this, and a row moving backwards one tick
after being claimed is the tracker working, not failing.

Each loader stores `0x30` or `0x18` beside its class pointer and I read that as

same `0x30` as everything else. The value does not vary with table complexity,

— the first was column 7 looking like `CashItem` on a 160x correlation. Both

## 2026-09-17 — what a compiled quest actually is

Followed the recorded probe into `CBasicQuest`. The answer came from the vtable
rather than the class: counting which slots the 153 compiled quests override
says what a quest *is*.

| slot | quests | median size | what it is |
|---|---|---|---|
| 20 | **153** | 31 | the scalar deleting destructor — **not** an interface method |
| 55 | 151 | 723 | **setup** |
| 22 | 85 | 1230 | the **dialogue handler** |
| 103 | 41 | 304 | |
| 1 | 35 | 769 | |

Slot 20 being universal looked at first like an identity method every quest must
implement. It is the destructor — the same `*this = vftable; if (flag & 1)
free(this)` shape that nearly became 209 `GetRefObjID` names in v0.1.255. Third
time this session that shape has had to be recognised rather than counted.

`CQuestBase` carries slots 5, 6, 9, 10, 11 and 12 as **4-byte stubs**, so a
quest that overrides nothing still has a working default for everything. That is
how 543 quests can exist with no compiled class at all.

### The binding is compiled too, not just the objectives

`CQNO_CH_POTION_4::vslot_055` (`0x008904a0`) carries as **string literals**:

	"NPC_CH_POTION"     the NPC it attaches to
	"NPC_CH_FERRY"  "NPC_CH_FERRY2"

So a quest has no row saying *offered by NPC X, requires quest Y* — it has a
compiled method naming them. This pushes the standing conclusion one level
further out: not only are objectives code, the quest's **prerequisites and NPC
attachment** are code. Yesterday's 85-table enumeration said no objective table
exists; this says no binding table would help either.

Slot 22 is the dialogue: `CQNO_CH_POTION_5::vslot_022` (`0x00890c60`) references
`SN_TALK_QNO_CH_POTION_5_01/07/09/10`, the quest's own lines resolved through

**Still open, and now precisely**: how the 543 classless quests attach to
anything, given attachment is a slot-55 override they do not have. Either the
generic path binds them from `_REFQUEST`, or they are not offered by NPCs at all
(event, tutorial and auto-granted quests would fit). That is the next probe, and
it is answerable by reading `CQuestBase`'s own slot-55 default.

## The reference-record field scanner is validated (2026-09-17)

**Tracker: 11 specified, 22 partial, 0 open, of 33.** The trailing number in the
entry above this one is stale — eleven systems moved between it and this entry
(Monster AI, alchemy, persistence, fortress war, guild, party, pets, academy,
jobs, durability, timed jobs, battle arena), each with a spec under
`docs/protocol/`, a Go package with tests, and names applied.

### What was blocked

`RefObjItem::ExtractData` (`0x006a3d50`, 7,052 bytes) is the single unread
function standing between two shipped specs and a real number: the packed
reinforce success rates in `alchemy.md` (`refRecord + (tier+21)*32`) and the
repair price basis in `durability.md` (`refRecord + 0xa4`). Both say "the offset
is read, the column is not".

`client/tools/re/fields.py` reads these deserializers mechanically — they consume
a record field by field from a cursor, bumping a column counter at `reader+0x28`
for each — so walking in address order gives field index → struct offset.

The previous tick shipped it **explicitly unvalidated**: against
`RefObjCommon_ExtractData`, whose 58-field count `refobj_binary_format.md` fixes
independently, it accounted for 47. The recorded next step was "explain eleven
fields".

### The eleven are explained, and the count now lands exactly

	40  inline counter bumps outside any loop
	 8  a 4-trip loop bumping twice per pass    -- the four requirement pairs
	 4  RefData_ReadStringField calls outside a loop
	 5  RefData_ReadStringField inside a 5-trip loop -- the five asset strings
	 1  FUN_006b1a80, the schema-driven field skipper
	--
	58

Six came from the requirement loop and five from the asset-string loop, both of
which the scanner had been counting as single fields.

**Three of the doc's own anchors land**, under one consistent convention (field
N, 1-based = text column N−1): the requirement pairs at fields 33..40 against
its columns 32..39, the asset strings at 53..57 against its 52..56, and field 58
at `+0x184` against its "58th and last common field". Three anchors from a
document written months earlier, agreeing with a scanner that knew nothing about
them.

### Three bugs, each of which produced a plausible wrong answer

Worth recording because none of them failed loudly:

1. **Loop trip counts.** A bump inside a loop executes once per iteration and
   appears once in the instruction stream. Counting instructions gave 43.
2. **Register-sourced trip counts.** The requirement loop sets its count with
   `mov eax,0x4` … `mov [esp+0x1c],eax` rather than an immediate store. Missing
   that form cost exactly six fields — 52 instead of 58.
3. **Pass ordering.** Building the stack-slot counter map in a pass of its own
   let a later `mov [esp+0x1c],ecx` (ecx = 1) overwrite the 4 the loop depends
   on. The value that matters is the one live *at the branch*, so it is one
   forward pass now.

A fourth had been fixed the tick before: the reader register is not fixed —
`esi` in `RefObjItem`, `edi` in `RefObjCommon` — and hardcoding one reported
**zero** fields for the other.

### Still not published, for two reasons

`RefObjItem::ExtractData` returns **153 fields, 79 offsets resolved**. The
validation covers the **count**, not the offsets, and two things block a column
claim:

- Resolved offsets run to `+0x298` and resume at `+0x524`. The gap holds exactly
  what the two specs want, because that region is written through walking
  pointers the tracker loses.
- **`+0xa4` and `+0xa8` are written by both `RefObjItem::ExtractData` and
  `RefObjCommon_ExtractData`.** Until it is settled which record
  `item->[0x34]->[0x18]` actually points at, a column index taken from either is
  a coin flip dressed as a recovery — the `characterdata` column-79 failure
  exactly.

So the next probe is narrow and stated: resolve the walking-pointer stores in
`0x2a0..0x520`, and settle which record `+0xa4` belongs to.

## `+0xa4` and `+0xa8` are common-record fields, and a second reader names one (2026-09-17)

The previous entry closed the field-count question and left two things open:
resolve the walking-pointer stores in `0x2a0..0x520`, and **settle which record
`+0xa4` belongs to** — flagged as a coin-flip risk, because the offset appeared
to be written by both `ExtractData` functions and a column index from the wrong
one would be wrong by the whole 58-field common prefix.

### The ownership question is closed

A `CRefObjItem` is **one object with two adjacent halves**:

	0x000 .. 0x184   RefObjCommon_ExtractData   -- the common record
	0x198 .. 0x53d   RefObjItem::ExtractData    -- the item record

The ranges are **disjoint**, and two independent facts establish it:

- Every `+0xa4` / `+0xa8` in `RefObjItem::ExtractData` is `[esp+0xa4]` /
  `[esp+0xa8]` — **stack locals, not record stores**. The apparent conflict was
  an artefact of matching on the offset without checking the base register.
- `RefObjCommon_ExtractData` writes `record+0xa4` and `record+0xa8` at
  `0x006a35e4` / `0x006a360f`, through a register traced back to the record
  pointer it spills to `[esp+0x14]` at entry.

So the repair price basis and the restore cost are **properties every game
object has**, and `alchemy.md`'s packed reinforce rates at
`0x2c0`/`0x2e0`/`0x300` are in the **item** half. Each spec now says which
deserializer its column index will come from.

### A second, unrelated reader confirms `+0xa8`

Exactly two functions read it, in different subsystems, with the same shape:

	if (!obj->vt[55]())   refuse;          // "can this be restored"
	cost = refRecord[0xa8];
	if (gold < cost)      refuse;
	gold -= cost;

`GObjNPCNPC::HandleRepairRequest` refuses `CANNOT_BE_REVIVED`;
`SiegeFortressMgr::HandleStructureRepair` (`0x00634950`, newly named) refuses
`FORT_BATTLEAIDE_REPAIR_FAIL`. **One field, two subsystems, the same vtable
slot 55 guard.** Reviving an item and rebuilding a fortress structure are the
same operation on the same common-record cost — a stronger reading than the item
path alone supported, and the reason `durability.md` no longer calls it "a flat
revive fee".

### Still not published: the column index

The scanner's identity propagation now resolves `+0xa4` (field 28) but **the
offset model is demonstrably wrong nearby**, so no index is claimed:

- The requirement loop's walking pointer advances by **8**, and the expansion
  uses the field size, so it reports `0xb4, 0xb8, 0xbc, 0xc0` where the real
  stores are `0xb4, 0xbc, 0xc4, 0xcc`.
- Propagating identity gained `+0xa4` and **lost the `+0x184` anchor**, because
  `mov ebx,[ebx+0x8]` reloads `ebx` from a *different* object and the tracker
  correctly drops it — so the two register strategies resolve different subsets.

The count is validated; the offsets are not, and this tick has a concrete
demonstration of how they fail rather than a suspicion. Next probe: make the
loop expansion use the walking pointer's own stride.

## Counting binary fields is a dead end past the common prefix (2026-09-17)

The recorded next probe was "make the loop expansion use the walking pointer's
own stride". That is done, a second ordering bug fell out with it, and together
they turned up a result that **redirects the effort rather than advancing it**.

### Two more scanner bugs, both producing right-looking wrong output

4. **Loop stride.** A loop's walking pointer advances by its own `add`, not by
   the field size. The requirement loop walks `ebx` by 8 and stores a dword at
   `[ebx-4]` and a byte at `[ebx]`; the field-size expansion reported
   `0xb4,0xb8,0xbc,0xc0` where the real stores are `0xb4,0xbc,0xc4,0xcc`.
5. **Multi-bump loop bodies interleave.** That loop consumes dword, byte, dword,
   byte … Emitting all iterations of the first store then all of the second
   gives the right offsets in the **wrong order**, and the order *is* the column
   map.

Fixed, the requirement pairs land as four `(dword, byte)` pairs at `0xb4/0xb8`,
`0xbc/0xc0`, `0xc4/0xc8`, `0xcc/0xd0` — which is what "four requirement pairs"
should look like, and the doc's columns 32..39 at fields 33..40.

### The dead end

Running the fixed scanner on all three deserializers:

| deserializer | binary fields | real text columns |
|---|---:|---:|
| `RefObjCommon_ExtractData` | 58 | — (a prefix) |
| `RefObjItem::ExtractData` | **153** | **160** |
| `RefObjChar_ExtractData` | **80** | **104** |

Both type-specific tables consume **fewer binary fields than their text has
columns** — item by 7, char by 24. So binary field order and text column order
agree only through the common prefix, exactly as `refobj_binary_format.md` said,
and **a type-specific offset cannot be turned into a text column by counting**.

That kills the plan `alchemy.md` was carrying for its packed reinforce rates.
The route that remains is the stream's own per-column schema — the
`(index, width)` records at `+0xe4`/`+0xe8`, stride `0x54`, that `FUN_006b1a80`
walks — and that is now the recorded probe.

`durability.md` is unaffected in principle: `+0xa4` is a **common** field, where
the two orders do agree, so `field N → text column N−1` applies to it.

### A column count was one too many, in two docs

itemdata was recorded as 161 columns and characterdata as 105. A natural
experiment settles both: `itemdata_1000` has **160** fields per line and **no
trailing tab**, while `itemdata_5000`, `_10000` and `_20000` have 161 and **every
line ends with a tab**. Splitting on tab turns that terminator into an empty
final field. The real counts are **itemdata 160** and **characterdata 104**.

**No recorded column index changes** — data still occupies 0..159 and 0..103.
Only the totals were wrong, and only by the one empty field. No Go value depends
on either number (`ItemCSVColumnCount` is srrevamp's own export width), so this
is a documentation correction.

### Still not published: the index for `+0xa4`

The scanner resolves it as field 28, which would be text column 27, and that is
**not** being claimed. Field 28 sits in a run whose offsets do not ascend with
the field order (27 → `+0x9c`, 28 → `+0xa4`, 29 → `+0xa8`, **30 → `+0xa0`**),
and no anchor brackets it. A struct need not be laid out in read order, so the
jump is not proof of error — but it removes the only sanity check there, and
itemdata columns 27 and 28 sit in a clean **1.5 ratio** that would make a wrong
answer look convincing. That is the `characterdata` column-79 shape exactly.

What would settle it: resolve the offset for field 15, which the doc anchors as
"Country at column 14", bracketing field 28 from below.

### The limitation now named

The scanner is a **linear pass with no control flow**. A register set on an
untaken branch is still attributed afterwards, which is why the `+0x184` anchor
cannot be recovered — field 58's store through `ebx` is real, but an earlier
`mov ebx,esi` on a different path drops the tracker's identity for `ebx`.

## The database column names are in the binary (2026-09-17)

The recorded probe was the stream's per-column schema — the `(index, width)`
records `FUN_006b1a80` walks — as the last route to a type-specific column
index. Reading it produced something better than the index, and also closed the
index question for good.

### The record carries a NAME

`Database::BuildStatement` (`0x009732f0`, newly named) builds `SELECT`,
`INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `WHERE` from those records, so they must hold column
names, and reading the loop gives the layout:

| offset | what |
|---|---|
| `+0x04` | the column **name**, an SSO `std::string` |
| `+0x24` | the column **width** |
| `+0x2c` | an ODBC-reported value |
| `+0x30` | the column **index** |
| `+0x34` | a flag: `1` excludes the column from `INSERT` |

### The index is runtime, the name is static

`Database::BindTableSchema` (`0x00972b40`, newly named) binds a table by
**name**: it fetches column metadata over ODBC, walks the records comparing each
declared name against the ODBC one with `CompareStringA`, and on a match writes
the **ODBC column index** into `+0x30`.

So **the executable declares the names and the live database supplies the
ordinals.** `ODBC32.dll` is imported by ordinal, 18 functions.

That closes the question the last three ticks were circling from the other side:
a static column index is not recoverable from the binary **because the binary
does not have one**. It matches by name and takes whatever position the database
reports. Both routes are now exhausted, and for a good reason rather than a
missing technique.

### The names themselves — 310 identifiers, 54 tables

They sit in a contiguous, 4-byte-aligned string pool at `.rdata`
**`0x00b11b08`–`0x00b12a70`**, extracted into `server/internal/persistence`
(`ColumnPool`, `TableColumns`, `SchemaTableOrder`) with tests, and written up in
`docs/protocol/db_columns.md`.

**The pool is deduplicated** — each name appears once, at first use — so a table
gets the names it *introduces*, not its full column list. `_TIMEDJOBFORPET` and
`_INVENTORYFORAVATAR` introduce nothing at all, reusing `_TIMEDJOB`'s and
`_INVENTORY`'s. That is stated wherever the list is used, and a test asserts the
empty ones stay empty.

### What it closes in four shipped specs

| spec | was unrecovered | now named |
|---|---|---|
| `timed_jobs.md` | "what the thirteen non-timestamp columns are" | `Category`, `JobID`, `TimeToKeep`, `Data3`…`Data8`, `JID` |
| `siege.md` | the dungeon caps, "read from a structure, not a literal" | `_SiegeFortress.CreatedDungeonCount` / `.CreatedDungeonTime` — so the cap is a per-fortress **database column**, i.e. server configuration, which is why no literal exists |
| `academy.md` | which membership branch is the master role | `_TRAININGCAMPMEMBER.MemberClass` |
| `academy.md` | the honour economy | `HonorPoint`, `Rank`, `GraduateCount`, `EvaluationPoint`, `LatestEvaluationDate`, `Ranking` |
| `guild.md` | where the permission mask lives | `_GUILDMEMBER.Permission` — and `SiegeAuthority` is a **separate column**, so fortress rights are not bits of that mask |

**These are names, not values.** Naming the field a cap is compared against is
not knowing the cap, and every spec says so where it cites one. The siege entry
is the most useful of the five precisely because it explains an absence: the
number was never in the binary to find.

`_CHAR`'s 42 introduced columns are the full character-persistence schema and
are the most directly useful of the lot for srrevamp.

## The reference tables have no column names, and that closes the question (2026-09-17)

The previous entry recovered the binary's schema pool — 310 identifiers, 54
tables — and noted `_CHAR`'s 42 columns as the most directly useful. This tick
asked the obvious follow-up: **is there a pool for the 85 reference tables?**

### No, and the absence is the answer

The `_REF*` names sit elsewhere in `.rdata` as a **bare run of table names with
nothing between them** — table name, table name, table name — while each of the
54 runtime tables carries its columns. A cross-check confirms it: **not one of
the 85 reference tables appears in the schema pool**, and a test now asserts
that.

`Database::BuildStatement` explains why. A table with no column records is
queried with

	SELECT * FROM %s

and the reference loaders consume the result **positionally**, through the
field-by-field `ExtractData` deserializers. The server never needs a reference
table's column names, so the binary does not carry them.

**This closes the item-column question for good.** Three ticks looked for a way
to name or index `_REFOBJITEM`'s columns — first by counting binary fields, then
by the per-column schema. Neither could work, and the reason is now a single
fact rather than two separate failures: *the server does not know those names
either.* A reference-table column is identifiable only by its **offset in the
deserialised record**, which `client/tools/re/fields.py` reads and which
`alchemy.md` and `durability.md` already cite. `alchemy.md` now says the line of
enquiry is closed rather than parked.

### The runtime table list was 35 and should have been 54

Cross-checking the pool against `persistence.RuntimeTables` found twenty tables
missing. The cause is exact and dull: the original harvest used
`_[A-Z][A-Z0-9_]{3,}` — **uppercase only** — and **all twenty it missed are
mixed-case**. `_SiegeFortress`, `_CharTrijob`, `_FleaMarketNetwork`, `_Friend`,
`_Memo` and fifteen more.

`RuntimeTables` is now the schema pool's own table order, with a test holding
the two equal so it cannot drift back to a hand-maintained list. The total is
**139 tables** — 85 reference, 54 runtime — not 120.

### `_LOADED` is not a table

It was in the old 35, and `persistence.md` hedged that it "may be a flag rather
than a table". **It is absent from the schema pool**, which resolves the hedge:
the server binds a schema for every runtime table it uses, and it binds none for
`_LOADED`. Dropped, with a test that fails if it returns.

`_DUMMY`, hedged the same way, **is** in the pool and stays.

### What this tick did not do

No value changed that srrevamp computes with — the corrections are to a table
list and to three documents. The one behavioural claim, that reference columns
are consumed positionally, is a restatement of what
`refobj_binary_format.md` already established from the other end.

## srrevamp's character model, mapped against the engine's `_CHAR` (2026-09-17)

The schema pool's most directly useful entry was `_CHAR`'s 42 columns, and it
had been recovered but not used. This tick used it.

`server/internal/character/schema.go` now holds the engine's column list and a
field-by-field mapping, with tests that fail if a `Character` field is added
without an entry, if a mapped column is not a real one, if any of the 42 goes
unaccounted for, or if the list drifts from `persistence.TableColumns["_CHAR"]`.

### Two naming confirmations

srrevamp's `Str` and `Int` are the engine's **`Strength`** and **`Intellect`**.
Small, but it is the difference between a convention and a citation.

### Two divergences, now named rather than incidental

- **`Gender` is not a column.** Race and sex follow from `RefObjID`, the
  reference object a character is built from. srrevamp stores a string because
  it selects asset paths directly.
- **`StorageGold` is not on the character.** Warehouse gold is the separate
  `_CHEST` table.

### A justification that rested on an assumption, corrected

`internal/mana` did not persist current MP and argued that "being topped up on
mana should not be worth reconnecting for, because the pool refills anyway",
which reads as though the design followed the game.

**`_CHAR` carries an `MP` column immediately beside `HP`.** The real server
persists current mana; relogging does not refill it there.

The choice stands — srrevamp has no cross-session consequence that turns on a
mana total — but it is **own design**, and it is recorded as one with a test
that keeps it stated. This is the third time a claim about the engine has rested
on a plausible assumption rather than a reading, and the shape is the same every
time: the design was fine, the justification was not.

### What the engine keeps that srrevamp models nowhere

Thirty of the 42, listed in `docs/protocol/character_schema.md`. The two worth
flagging:

- **Five columns for the return point and five for the death point**
  (`TelRegion`/`TelPos*`/`TelWorldID`, `DiedRegion`/`DiedPos*`/`DiedWorldID`).
  The engine treats "where you go back to" and "where you died" as first-class
  persisted state.
- **`HwanLevel` is persisted**, which is worth holding against the berserk work
  in `param_registry.md`: the gauge is transient, the level is not.

No value srrevamp computes with changed. What changed is that every field on
`Character` is now either matched to the engine's own name or recorded as a
deliberate divergence, and the next field added has to answer the same question.

## Two open probes retired, one of them for the right reason (2026-09-17)

Spent the tick on the census the goal actually asks for — *which values srrevamp
ships that are still own design, and which of them a readable table or a code
path could ground* — and two entries resolved.

### `masteryUpCost` was already recovered; the tracker row was stale

`SYSTEMS.md` said of Skills and masteries: *"mastery cost `masteryUpCost` is own
design; find its use-site"*. Both halves are wrong. The use-site was found —
`FUN_0059c4e0`, the mastery level-up handler, which walks the levels being raised
and accumulates the level table's `entry+0x10` — and the value is real, served
from leveldata's column 2 (1, 1, 2, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 12 … 53 at level 20, 172 at
32). Only the **no-table fallback** is own design.

The row now says so, and points at what actually remains own design there:
`DisclosedSkillDamagePerLevel`.

This is the rot `internal/systems` exists to catch, and it is the half the test
cannot catch: the checker verifies that an unfinished row *has* a next probe, not
that the probe is still open. Worth knowing about the guard's limits.

### Inventory's starting size: there is no write, so there is nothing to find

`internal/inventory` explained its own-design `SlotsPerCharacter = 50` with
*"nothing in the dump writes +0x1c2c — the write reaches it through a register —
so the STARTING size is still unrecovered"*. That implies a write exists and the

Searching the **disassembly** rather than the decompiler's output shows there is

- All **ten** instructions referencing `+0x1c2c` are READS, in

One loose end is recorded rather than assumed: `_charnamelist` and
